issues.legal_issue: An award of an inter-State water disputes tribunal may be challenged before the Supreme Court by special leave.
material_facts: States aggrieved by the tribunal's final water-allocation award challenged it in civil appeals by special leave.
The Court had previously held that the provision giving the tribunal's award the same force as a Supreme Court order did not exclude the Court's jurisdiction under Article 136.
issues.conclusion: The appeals by special leave were maintainable.
issues.legal_principle: Section 6(2) of the Inter-State Water Disputes Act, 1956 gives the tribunal's award binding effect and enables it to be executed or abided by as if it were a decree of the Supreme Court; it does not bar Article 136 jurisdiction. Section 11 and Article 262 concern exclusion of jurisdiction over the water dispute itself, and do not create an absolute bar to an appeal under Article 136. The Court relied on its earlier decision in State of Karnataka v. State of Tamil Nadu (2017).

predicates.appeal_against_water_disputes_award: A party to an inter-State water dispute appealed against the award made in that dispute.
predicates.award_has_binding_implementation_effect: The award is binding and is to be implemented as though it were an order of the Supreme Court.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges a binding inter-State water-dispute award, the appeal may be brought by special leave.

issues.legal_issue: Non-political agreements concerning the sharing and use of water did not lapse merely because British paramountcy ended or the Constitution came into force.
material_facts: The agreements regulated irrigation, reservoirs, and the sharing and use of water between the predecessor governments.
The agreements were not denounced, and the successor governments continued to act under them.
issues.conclusion: The agreements did not become extinct on the lapse of paramountcy or the commencement of the Constitution.
issues.legal_principle: Section 7(1)(b) of the Indian Independence Act, 1947 concerned political treaties and agreements and did not extinguish these ordinary water-sharing agreements. The Court relied on the Standstill Agreement, the absence of denunciation, and the distinction between political instruments and ordinary agreements. It considered State of Tamil Nadu v. State of Kerala (2014), Dr. Babu Ram Saksena v. State, and H.H. Maharajadhiraja Madhav Rao Jivaji Rao Scindia Bahadur v. Union of India.

rule.if: inter_state_water_sharing_dispute and agreement_is_nonpolitical and no_denunciation_or_replacement and successor_states_continued_performance

predicates.inter_state_water_sharing_dispute: The proceeding concerns competing states' use, distribution, or control of water from an inter-State river.
predicates.agreement_is_nonpolitical: The agreement regulates ordinary matters such as water sharing, irrigation, or reservoirs rather than a political settlement or matter of sovereignty.
predicates.no_denunciation_or_replacement: Neither side denounced the agreement or replaced it with a later agreement.
predicates.successor_states_continued_performance: The successor governments continued to act under the agreement.

issues.definition: A non-political water-sharing agreement survives a political transition when it is neither denounced nor replaced and successor governments continue to act under it.

issues.legal_issue: The constitutional bar concerning certain agreements with former rulers does not apply to disputes arising from ordinary water-sharing agreements.
material_facts: The dispute concerned agreements regulating water use, irrigation, and reservoirs.
The agreements did not concern sovereignty, the integrity of India, or a political settlement.
issues.conclusion: Article 363 did not bar adjudication of the dispute on the basis of the agreements.
issues.legal_principle: Article 363 excludes jurisdiction over disputes arising from political treaties and similar instruments, not ordinary agreements. The Court distinguished State of Seraikella v. Union of India, which concerned a political dispute involving an Instrument of Accession, and relied on H.H. Maharajadhiraja Madhav Rao Jivaji Rao Scindia Bahadur v. Union of India and State of Tamil Nadu v. State of Kerala (2014).

predicates.inter_state_water_dispute: The proceeding concerns competing states' use, distribution, or control of water from an inter-State river.
predicates.dispute_relies_on_ordinary_water_sharing: A party relies on an agreement about water use, irrigation, or reservoirs that is not political in nature.

issues.definition: The constitutional bar does not apply when an inter-State water dispute relies on an ordinary, non-political water-sharing agreement.

issues.legal_issue: The historical disparity in bargaining power did not make the water-sharing agreements unconscionable and void.
material_facts: The agreements had been acted upon for decades, and the successor state had obtained benefits under them.
After the political transition, the successor state did not denounce or challenge the agreements while it had the opportunity to do so.
The successor state raised the challenge after the agreements had been acted upon for a long period.
issues.conclusion: The agreements were not void for unconscionability.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 16, 19, and 19A of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, unequal bargaining power may be relevant to whether an agreement is unconscionable, but inequality alone does not invalidate it. The Court relied on Central Inland Water Transport Corporation Ltd. v. Brojo Nath Ganguly, O.P. Bhandari v. ITDC, Delhi Transport Corporation v. D.T.C. Mazdoor Congress, and Balmer Lawrie & Co. Ltd. v. Partha Sarathi Sen Roy. It concluded that the later opportunity to bargain or challenge, coupled with continued performance and absence of denunciation, defeated the challenge in this case.

predicates.inter_state_water_sharing_dispute: The proceeding concerns competing states' use, distribution, or control of water from an inter-State river.
predicates.agreement_performed_after_political_tran: The successor governments continued to act under the agreement after the political transition.
predicates.successor_state_had_opportunity_to_chall: The successor state had the ability to bargain over, denounce, or challenge the agreement after the political transition.
predicates.successor_state_did_not_denounce_agreeme: The successor state did not denounce or challenge the agreement while that opportunity existed.

issues.definition: An agreement is not void for unconscionability on the basis of historical bargaining inequality when it continued to be performed after the successor state had an opportunity to challenge it and the state did not do so.

issues.legal_issue: A territorial reorganization that does not change sovereignty does not automatically extinguish existing agreements binding on the predecessor state.
material_facts: The reorganization altered state territories and created a new state, but did not involve a change of sovereignty.
The agreement continued to be recognized and acted upon after reorganization and was not repudiated.
issues.conclusion: The agreements continued to bind the successor state.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 107 and 119 of the States Reorganisation Act, 1956, together with Article 295(2) of the Constitution, supported continuity of existing rights, liabilities, and obligations. The Court also relied on the principle that laws and administrative arrangements continue after territorial reorganization unless modified, changed, or repudiated. It referred to State of Punjab v. Balbir Singh and Ranjan Sinha v. Ajay Kumar Vishwakarma.

predicates.inter_state_water_dispute: The proceeding concerns competing states' use, distribution, or control of water from an inter-State river.
predicates.territorial_reorganization_without_sover: The boundaries or territories of states were reorganized without a change of sovereignty.
predicates.successor_state_did_not_repeal_or_reject: The successor state neither repealed nor repudiated the agreement.

issues.definition: An existing agreement remains binding after territorial reorganization when sovereignty is unchanged and the successor state does not repeal or reject it.

issues.legal_issue: The 1924 agreement expired after its specified fifty-year term because the provisions open to reconsideration were essential parts of the agreement and no mutual continuation was agreed.
material_facts: The agreement provided that specified limitations and arrangements would be open to reconsideration after fifty years and to modifications or additions mutually agreed upon.
The parties did not reach a mutual agreement to continue or modify those arrangements after the specified term.
issues.legal_principle: The agreement had to be construed as a whole, giving effect to the language that specified arrangements were open to reconsideration and that modifications or additions required mutual agreement. The Court concluded that the clauses subject to reconsideration were essential to the agreement and that its terms did not indicate permanence. It did not treat the earlier Presidential Reference's statements about expiry as a decision of the specific issue.

predicates.inter_state_water_sharing_dispute: The proceeding concerns competing states' use, distribution, or control of water from an inter-State river.
predicates.agreement_sets_fixed_term_reconsideratio: The agreement makes essential limitations or arrangements open to reconsideration after a specified term.
predicates.no_mutual_continuation_or_modification: The parties do not mutually agree to continue or modify the arrangements after that term.

issues.definition: An agreement expires at the end of its fixed term when essential arrangements are subject to reconsideration then and the parties do not mutually agree to continue or modify them.

issues.legal_issue: Expiry of the agreement did not prevent adjudication of the referred water dispute.
material_facts: The complaint described a water dispute involving executive action, projects, diminished water supply, and failed negotiations, in addition to alleged breaches of the agreements.
The dispute had been referred for adjudication and had proceeded through extensive tribunal proceedings.
The complaint did not use the precise words that the state's interests had been prejudicially affected.
issues.conclusion: The Court rejected the contention that the complaint should be dismissed without adjudication and proceeded to determine the dispute on its merits.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3 of the Inter-State Water Disputes Act, 1956 permits a state to seek a reference where its or its inhabitants' interests in inter-State waters have been or are likely to be prejudicially affected by specified conduct. The Court assessed the complaint in light of its antecedents, the reference, and the course of proceedings, and declined to dismiss it merely because the agreement had expired or the complaint did not use the exact statutory phrase.

predicates.inter_state_water_dispute_reference: A state has sought and obtained a reference of a dispute concerning an inter-State river for adjudication.
predicates.complaint_describes_water_related_prejud: The complaint describes conduct or failures said to harm the state's or its inhabitants' interests in the river's waters.
predicates.dispute_was_referred_for_adjudication: The dispute was referred to a tribunal and has proceeded as an adjudicable water dispute.

issues.definition: A referred inter-State water dispute requires merits adjudication when the complaint describes water-related prejudice, even if it does not use the precise statutory wording.

issues.legal_issue: Inter-State river waters must be apportioned equitably among riparian states rather than treated as the exclusive property of any one state.
material_facts: Several riparian states and a union territory asserted competing claims to the waters of the same inter-State river.
The available water was insufficient to meet all claimed and projected uses.
The agreements were not a continuing basis for allocation after the Court held that the 1924 agreement had expired.
issues.conclusion: The dispute had to be decided on the basis of the equal status of the states and equitable apportionment, with each state's share determined on the facts rather than by a claim of exclusive ownership or an automatic equal division.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(c) of the Inter-State Water Disputes Act, 1956 defines a water dispute, and Section 3 provides for complaints where state or inhabitants' interests are prejudicially affected. Article 262 provides for adjudication of such disputes. The Court relied on the principle stated in In re Presidential Reference (Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal), Kansas v. Colorado, and the Helsinki Rules, 1966: riparian states have equal standing, no state has exclusive ownership of flowing inter-State waters, and equitable shares depend on the relevant circumstances and needs. Equality of status does not require equal quantities.

predicates.inter_state_water_apportionment_proceedi: The proceeding concerns allocation of water from a river flowing through more than one state.
predicates.multiple_riparian_claimants: More than one state or territory claims a share of the river's waters.
predicates.available_water_is_competing: The available water cannot satisfy all claimed or projected uses without an allocation.

issues.definition: When multiple riparian claimants compete for insufficient inter-State river water, their shares are determined by equitable apportionment.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court should decide the dispute rather than remit it to the tribunal for fresh consideration.
material_facts: More than twenty-seven years had elapsed since the tribunal was constituted.
All party states were before the Supreme Court and had challenged the final award.
Counsel for all parties agreed that remand would not resolve the dispute and that the Court should decide the legal and factual issues.
issues.conclusion: The Court proceeded to decide the legal and factual issues instead of remitting the matter to the tribunal.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on its plenary powers under Articles 136 and 142 of the Constitution and considered the elapsed time, the presence of all parties, and the agreed view that remand would be futile.

predicates.appeal_from_water_disputes_award: The proceeding is an appeal challenging an inter-State water-disputes award.
predicates.all_disputing_parties_are_before_supreme: All parties to the water dispute are before the Supreme Court.
predicates.remand_would_be_futile: The parties and the Court consider that returning the matter to the tribunal would not resolve the dispute effectively.

issues.definition: The Supreme Court decides an appealed water dispute without remand when all disputing parties are before it and remand would be futile.
